# The canonical register: Ginnungagap

*Court is in session. In the matter of Ginnungagap, the register hears the evidence — the attestation, the marks, and the forms that stand accused.*

## At a Glance

- **Canonical form:** Ginnungagap
- **Original script:** ᚴᛁᚾᚾᚢᚾᚴᛅᚴᛅᛒ
- **Pantheon:** Norse
- **Convention:** normalized Old Norse spelling — þ, ð, ǫ, æ and length marks preserved as the editions print them
- **False forms on record:** 0
- **Contested forms:** none attested
- **Series:** The Canonical Register, No. 141 of 406

## The Charge

That the name **Ginnungagap** is routinely written in forms that move, drop, or invent its marks — and that each such form teaches the reader a different, lesser name. The register's task is to separate the honest fallback from the outright false.

## The Defense of the Canonical Form

The attested form is **ᚴᛁᚾᚾᚢᚾᚴᛅᚴᛅᛒ**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Ginnungagap**.

No diacritics are required here: the canonical form is the exactness of the spelling itself, the form normalized Old Norse spelling — þ, ð, ǫ, æ and length marks preserved as the editions print them demands.

## The Character Witness

The plain form *ginnungagap* differs from the canonical **Ginnungagap** only by convention of display — case, not content. It is **acceptable everywhere**: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

## Mitigating Circumstances

No alternate form of this name carries documented scholarly support in the lexicon's record. The convention here — normalized Old Norse spelling — þ, ð, ǫ, æ and length marks preserved as the editions print them — produces exactly one defensible transliteration: **Ginnungagap**. Forms that differ from it are not contested; they are simply wrong.

## The Convention's Own History

Old Norse orthography is a primary source in itself: þ (thorn) and ð (eth) are letters the language used natively, not transliteration marks — English once had them too, and lost them. ǫ (o with ogonek) is a nasal vowel with its own saga-era history, and normalized Old Norse spelling preserves it because the Eddas' editors do. To write th for þ or o for ǫ is not modernization; it is a different spelling of a different word. The Eddic poems survive in one manuscript tradition each — the register spells the names the way those manuscripts do.

## Registration, Honestly

Three facts govern every domain this project registers. One: IDNA 2008 welcomes the marks — punycode encodes them legally and browsers show them faithfully. Two: welcome is not availability — registrars hold partial inventory, so the ideal form of a name may exist in the protocol yet not in the shop window today. Three: typeability is a separate virtue — a form no one can type on a phone is a form no one will visit, however canonical.

Hence the hierarchy the rulebook enforces: take the most complete form that is *both* attested and *actually registrable*, and never accept a wrong mark for the sake of availability. The wrong accent is not a rung on that ladder; it is off the ladder entirely.

## The Verdict

So the register finds: **Ginnungagap**, canonical; *ginnungagap*, equally canonical; the contested forms, recorded with their support; the false forms, ruled against with their violations named. Every line of that finding cites its evidence, and the evidence is open to any reader — the register asks to be checked, not trusted. The temple keeps the canonical form at [/ginnungagap/](/ginnungagap/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 7 cited sources — Poetic Edda: Völuspá 3 (gap ginnunga, grass nowhere), Vafþrúðnismál 21 (Élivágar and the quickening of Ymir), Grímnismál 40–41 (the world made from Ymir's body), Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 4–9 (Niflheimr and Hvergelmir, the Élivágar, Muspellsheimr and Surtr, the mildness of Ginnungagap, the quickening of Ymir and Auðhumla, the killing of Ymir, the world fashioned in the gap), Hesiod, Theogony 116 (Chaos first of all) — the Greek parallel of the yawning beginning.
